title: A pricing page for an education product
metaTitle: Education product pricing page: show the fit
excerpt: Show what a class or a trial includes, what it does not, and the shape of the price. A tired teacher or parent is judging fit, not doing arithmetic.
alt: An OPEN sign hanging in a shop window, with the word SHOP printed on the glass, as plain as a price should be.
caption: An OPEN sign in a shop window, with SHOP printed on the glass. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Does an education pricing page have to show a number?
faqs.answer: It has to show the shape. Families and single classes can usually see a price or a clear range. A school quote can list the factors, such as teachers, students, and training, instead of a blank contact line with no edges.

faqs.question: What should a trial state up front?
faqs.answer: How long it lasts, whether it is the real lesson, whether a card is required, and what happens on the last day. A trial that quietly becomes a paid plan is a trap. Parents and teachers remember traps.

faqs.question: How should family, class, and school offers differ?
faqs.answer: They are different products even when they share content. Separate blocks should say who supervises, what the adult sees, and which action starts that version. Do not hide the differences in a toggle and small type.

markdown:
An education product pricing page is where a teacher or a parent with little time decides whether the product fits. It is not where they do arithmetic. Show what is included, what is not, and how to start a class or a trial.

Do not hide the shape of the price if the buyer will ask anyway. "Contact sales" as the only line tells a parent you are not for them, and it tells a teacher they will have to wait through a pitch before they learn if the tool is even in range.

## Fit before the calculator

Open with who each price is for. A family practicing at home. A teacher running one class. A school buying for a grade. If you only sell one of those, say so in the first sentence and do not draw empty columns for the others. Empty columns are how education pages pretend to be a platform.

The buyer is asking three questions, in this order. Is this the version that matches my role. What do I get before I am locked in. What would I pay if it works. Answer them in that order. A giant number with no role attached answers the third question for the wrong person.

[Google's people-first guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) asks whether a page helps someone finish a real task. Choosing a class or a trial is the task. A pricing page written to avoid saying a number, or written as a slogan about "investing in learners," fails the task. Write the offer. You can still be careful with words.

Name the unit in language they use. Per child. Per class. Per school, if that is a real contract and not a wish. Say the period. A month. A school year. A single course. "Seat" is vendor language. Use it only if your buyers already say it. Many teachers do not.

Keep the page quiet. No flashing discount. No shame about the free option if you have one. A free classroom plan can be the honest fit for a teacher who is trying the lesson before they ask an administrator for money. Hiding it to push a trial with a card is a short-term trick and a long-term support problem.

## The shape of the price

Show the shape even when the final school contract is a conversation. Families can see a price. A single class can see a price or a clear range. A district can see what changes the quote: number of teachers, number of students, training, a data agreement. "Custom" without those factors is a fog machine.

A trial should have a shape too. How many days. Whether it is the real product or a reduced tour. Whether a card is required. What happens on the last day. A trial that rolls into a paid plan without a plain sentence is not a trial. It is a trap, and parents talk about traps.

If the price changes with the length of the commitment, show both and say what each is for. Monthly for a family that wants to stop in the summer. A school year for a teacher who does not want to re-approve in October. Do not make the cheaper-looking number a decoy that excludes the feature the homepage just promised. The homepage and the price have to describe the same lesson.

Discounts for a real reason can be stated. A title I school. A second child in the same household. Do not invent a crossed-out price that nobody pays. Teachers notice. It makes the rest of the page feel like a store they do not trust with a classroom.

You do not need to publish Hanabi's prices or anyone else's. You need to publish yours, in the form you will still honor on the call. If you are not ready to honor a number, publish the unit, the included list, and the single step that produces a number. Then keep that promise in writing.

## Included, and not included

Each offer needs both lists. Included is what they picture using this week. The lessons or the practice. The teacher view, if the plan has one. The parent view, if the plan has one. Rosters, if you are selling a class. Offline or printing, if you truly support it. A way to get help from a person.

Not included is what will otherwise become an angry email. A guarantee of grade improvement. A human tutor, unless you sell one. Devices. A full curriculum for every subject if you only cover one skill. Training for the whole staff, if training is a separate line. Student data shared with anyone beyond what the policy says. Write the limit next to the promise.

Content boundaries matter in this category more than in ordinary software. Which grades. Which skills. Which language. Whether you are the lesson or a supplement to their lesson. A teacher buying "math" who finds only one unit on fractions will feel misled even if the fractions unit is excellent. Say the unit. Let the excellence be on the product page.

Updates belong on the list if they are part of the price. New lessons during the year. A frozen course that will not grow. Either can be fair. Silence is what makes people assume the more generous one. Assume they will assume, and write it down.

The start of a class or a trial should say what they must supply. Email. A class name. Consent if a child is involved. You are not selling a mystery box. The price is also a preview of the setup. If setup takes a week of IT, the teacher plan is not a teacher plan. Move it to the school column and say why.

## Trial, class, and school

These are different products even when they share content. Give them different rows or blocks, not one toggle that hides the differences in small type.

A family trial or plan: who supervises, how long a session is, the price, how to cancel, and the fact that a parent does not have to teach the skill if that is true. The action is to start a trial or start the practice tonight.

A teacher class: the size you priced, the time to run the first activity, whether students need accounts, and what the teacher sees. The action is to start a class. If an administrator must pay, say that before they build a roster they cannot keep.

A school or district: the factors in the quote, what training includes, what you will not customize, and how to talk to a person. The action might be a conversation rather than an instant class. Label it as a conversation. Do not send a principal through a consumer checkout and call it simple.

Order the blocks by the buyer you most need, not by the largest contract. If the product is genuinely for parents, lead with parents. A huge "enterprise" slab above a family price tells parents they are an afterthought. They will act like one.

A short set of questions under the blocks can do the work of a sales call for the simple paths. Can I try one lesson first. Can I use it on a phone. What if I teach two classes. What happens to the work if we cancel. Answer in sentences. Link to the policy for privacy. Do not paste the policy in full on the pricing page.

## What a tired buyer looks for

They look for the number, the unit, and the catch. Design so those three are visible without a hover and without a comparison chart that only makes sense on a wide screen. Stack the offers on a phone. Repeat the action on each. A parent in a car line will not pinch a six-column matrix.

They look for whether the learning moment from the homepage is inside the price they can afford. If the homepage showed a teacher dashboard and the cheap plan has no teacher view, say it in the not-included list in plain type, not in a footnote. Footnotes are where trust goes to thin out.

They look for a human if the decision is a school decision. Put the path to a person near the school price, with what to have ready: roughly how many classes, which grade, whether you need a data agreement. Do not make them hunt to a generic contact page and re-explain the product.

They do not look for your cost of goods, your story about building the company, or a lecture about how education is underpriced. Those paragraphs feel like a prelude to a number you are nervous about. Print the number, or print the shape. Then stop.

## Where the page should send them

End on the start, in the same words as the button. Start a class, or start a trial. Under it, one line on what the first session contains, so the price and the lesson stay connected. A buyer who understands the price and forgets the lesson will churn. A buyer who loves the lesson and feels tricked by the price will be angry. The page should leave them with both.

If a school buyer needs a person, the path is a call, not a maze. Book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min) when you want a studio to look at how the offer is framed, not as the button label for every parent. Your own page should use your action. Hanabi's call is for founders who are building the product and the site, and it should decide whether the pricing page is saying the true shape.

Before you publish, read every included item against the product you can ship this month. Delete promises that live only on the page. Add limits you have been explaining in email. The email is the draft of the not-included list. Move it into the open.

The next page, if the offers still sound like internal tiers, is the services or plans page in the buyer's language. [The services page an education product actually needs](/blog/the-services-page-an-education-product-actually-needs) gives each offer an outcome, a boundary, and a next step. Pricing says what it costs. That page says what the work is. A teacher should not have to infer one from the other.
